harness:
On the kept branch, under `spikes/relations/`: `harness.py` (every stage), `sandbox.py` (the refusal every write passes), `test_sandbox.py` (the offline proof of that refusal: `python3 -B -m unittest discover -s spikes/relations -p 'test_*.py'`).

**The one command:** `python3 spikes/relations/harness.py all [--stamp S] [--keep]`, or `harness.py <stage>...`, needing `GH_PROJECTS_TOKEN` and `LINEAR_API_KEY` in `~/.config/onetaskgraph/secrets.env`. Stages run in `STAGES` order; `all` runs them and then always runs `cleanup` however a stage ended. `sandbox.Sandbox.check_github` and `check_linear` refuse, before anything is sent, any write outside the two scratch repositories, a board this run did not create, a Linear team other than `TES2`/`TES`, an issue or relation this run did not create, or an unstamped title. No credential is written; evidence holds operation names, costs, ids, numbers, and only the synthetic bodies quoted below. The evidence of this run is `spikes/relations/evidence/20261108T180000/`: `requests.jsonl` (one row per request, the numbers cited below as "request N"), one `<stage>.json` per stage, `ledger.jsonl`, `gates.jsonl` and `pages/*.png`. Two questions a review left open were answered afterwards under the same stamp, by `python3 spikes/relations/harness.py relation_gaps --stamp 20261108T180000 --keep` (`relation_gaps.json`, `relation_gaps_cleanup.json`): that stage deletes only what it created, so it neither overwrites `cleanup.json` nor sends `#6094` another delete.
method:
Run stamp `20261108T180000`, against real GitHub (schema introspected at request 5, 2026-11-08) and real Linear GraphQL (introspected at request 6, 2026-11-08), on sandbox destinations: GitHub issues titled with the stamp in `nickderobertis/onetaskgraph-live-scratch` and, for cross-repository questions, `onetaskgraph-live-scratch-2`; nine boards the spike created (`onetaskgraph live board spike-relations-20261108T180000-*`, across the coexistence and fallback stages and their reruns, every one deleted); Linear issues and projects in team `TES2`, and `TES` for cross-team questions. Every write is in `ledger.jsonl`. Today's real plugin was driven by running this repository's built `target/debug/onetaskgraph` (version 0.14.9) as a subprocess against each board and team, in a private `HOME`.

**How cost was read.** A GitHub read's points are its `rateLimit.cost`. A mutation document cannot select `rateLimit`, and the `x-ratelimit-used` headers are confounded by other consumers of the same token (a delta of 1669 across one 12-alias write at request 546), so each mutation is counted as **1 point per document**, the delta observed on quiet windows (request 18, 19, 23 single `addSubIssue`; request 53, a 25-alias `addSubIssue`). Each row keeps its raw `used_delta`. On Linear each request's `x-complexity` is recorded. Report figures are per request.

**What stopped the first run, and what it shows.** The first GitHub session, at about one issue a second, sent 42 mutation documents carrying 123 `createIssue` and 119 `addSubIssue` aliases inside about four minutes, then every further request was answered **HTTP 403** with no rate-limit figures (request 62) while the primary limit still showed about 3,700 of 5,000 — the secondary limiter. The harness stopped GitHub at once, and after about 60 minutes (per the manager) sent one read and resumed with one issue creation per 3 s. So this is a measurement of what batched relation writes can sustain: a full plan's parents, creates and links, sustained, reach the secondary limit within minutes even at this rate; one relation batch of the planned size does not.

### 1. Parents and sub-issues

**GitHub.** Add `addSubIssue` (18, 254), read `parent`/`subIssues` (20–21, 256), remove `removeSubIssue` (26, 262). A move names a second parent: without `replaceParent` it is refused `Sub issue may only have one parent` (22, 258), with `replaceParent: true` it moves (23, 259, read 24). A cycle is refused `Sub issue may not create a circular dependency` (25, 261). **Depth and children-per-parent, GitHub's documented limits:** "You can add up to 100 sub-issues per parent issue and create up to eight levels of nested sub-issues." ([Adding sub-issues](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/adding-sub-issues), read 2026-11-09.) By the manager's ruling at the user's request the probe stopped there and no further issues were created to test these. **What was observed before that ruling, labelled as such, and consistent with the documentation:** *observed rejection, depth:* a chain of 8 levels (a root and 7 layers of sub-issues) was accepted and adding the 9th level was refused at request 37: `You can't add more than 7 layers of sub-issues. To add a sub-issue, remove a parent issue at any level.` *Observed rejection, children:* 100 sub-issues on one parent were accepted (requests 53–56, read back 100 at 58 and 264) and the next five were refused at request 57: `Parent cannot have more than 100 sub-issues`. **Cross-repository parent:** accepted, parent in the scratch repository and child in `onetaskgraph-live-scratch-2` (61, 267), read from both ends (268–269). An issue page shows a Sub-issues panel with progress and a timeline entry (`pages/children-parent.png`, `pages/hierarchy-parent.png`). In a Projects v2 table the hierarchy is an expander row and a `Sub-issues progress` column (`pages/board-table.png`); `PARENT_ISSUE` and `SUB_ISSUES_PROGRESS` are board field types (introspected, and read from a created board's fields at 485). **Sub-issues join a board by themselves:** a created board has the workflow `Auto-add sub-issues to project` enabled (485); a child added to a parent on the board appeared on it 20 s later, and a grandchild the same way (489, 491). **Cost:** 1 point per write and per read, including a 20-alias relation read at 544.

**Linear.** `issueUpdate(parentId)` adds, moves (no separate replace) and, with `parentId: null`, removes (66, 70, 73); a cycle is refused `invalid parent` (72). **Depth:** accepts at least 10 levels (requests 76–84, the full probe); the actual limit is not measured. **Children:** accepts at least 105 on one parent (requests 86–91, read back 105 at 92); the actual limit is not measured. **Cross-team parent:** accepted, child in `TES`, parent in `TES2` (94), read from both ends (95–96). **Cost:** 1 request, complexity 3, per parent write; 235 for a read of `parent`, `children`, `relations` and `inverseRelations` (68). How Linear's own UI shows the hierarchy is **unverified as a UI observation** (no signed-in session): the API reports `parent` and `children`, and Linear's documentation shows parent/sub-issue rows.

**Coexistence of the two GitHub meanings, today's real plugin against a `sub_issues: parent` reading (the final `gh_boards` run, requests 484–535, and `gh_plugin_project` 563–575; earlier runs of the stage stay in the log).** The real plugin reads an issue with sub-issues, or carrying the project marker, as a project; a filed issue is a task. *One board:* after parent writes (`cause` > `sym` > two clients), the default source's `project list` is `cause`, its `task list` is `sym`, `cl1`, `cl2` — the middle ticket `sym`, which has children, reads as a task, so its children are tasks of it only in the parent reading (`task show` of `cause` exits 1 `no task with that id`; `project show` answers). A default source therefore names a `parent` source's top ticket a project and flattens the hierarchy below it. `project status set` writes that ticket's board status (`cause` moves to In Progress, `pages/board-table.png`). Removing an edge changes the other view: after `removeSubIssue(cause, sym)` (510), `sym`, now with no parent and still with children, is a project in the default source. In the other direction `project copy` from a folder creates issue `#6283` with sub-issue `#6284` (gh_plugin_project); the parent reading sees an ordinary parent with one child, and `addSubIssue` onto it (570) adds a task the default source lists in that project. *Two boards sharing one repository:* before a shared issue exists the default source on the project board is untouched. Adding one parent ticket to that board changes it after the workflow runs: immediately it is unchanged, and 30 s later that ticket is a project and its sub-issues are tasks there (`two_default_on_y_*`). And one issue has one parent across both meanings: `addSubIssue` of a project's task under a ticket is refused without `replaceParent` (424, 529) and moves it with `replaceParent` (425, 530), after which its project on the other board reads as a task. **Safe arrangement:** a `sub_issues: parent` source on a board of its own, none of whose issues are ever added to a board read with the default meaning, with the expectation that any such issue placed on a default board is read as a project and its sub-issues join that board by the workflow. On one board the two meanings give different answers for the same issues, and adding or removing an edge from either side rewrites the other's view.

**Linear normalization of the section, through the API.** Sent `- **caused-by** → [TES2-…](…) `tes2:…`` then `* second bullet` before the slot; Linear stored the first bullet as `* **caused-by**…` with its inline link and code span intact, inserted two extra blank lines before the second bullet, and kept the HTML-comment slot byte for byte (request 200, the stored text at `fallback_stored_quote` in `li_links.json`). Heading, bold, link, code span and comment survive; `- ` becomes `* ` and blank lines change. So a section parser must accept `*` bullets and tolerate blank lines. That is the API's normalization; a human edit in Linear's editor is **unverified** (no signed-in session).

### 3. The symptoms-and-root-causes walk-through, live on Linear

Run at requests 214–235 on TES2: `stale-cache-lease` (TES2-2134), symptoms `TIMEOUT-42` (TES2-2135), `PAY-7` (TES2-2136) and `THIRD-9` (TES2-2140), client-symptoms `TIMEOUT-42/acme` (TES2-2137), `TIMEOUT-42/globex` (TES2-2138), `PAY-7/acme` (TES2-2139). Each client-symptom a sub-issue of its symptom (215–217); each symptom `related` to the root cause (218–220) beside `caused-by` metadata on both ends through `task metadata set`. Read back from both ends: the root cause's `inverseRelations` lists all three symptoms and its metadata holds three `in` edges; a symptom's `children` lists its client-symptoms, `parent` of a client names its symptom, and a symptom's `relations` names the root cause beside one `out` metadata edge. The third symptom's link leaves the root cause with three `caused-by` edges, the count the design's `widespread-root-cause` route tests; onefollowup itself did not run.

### 4. Judging the four complete configurations

- **single-root-cause:** expressible as written; it uses no parent or link setting.
- **symptoms-and-root-causes:** expressible as written on Linear, and confirmed by the walk-through (`store: parent` for `occurs-for`, `store: link` with `link_types: caused-by: {native: related}` for `caused-by`).
- **typed-destinations:** expressible as written; it uses no relation.
- **inline-fixes:** expressible as written; it uses no relation.

No change is needed for the four as written. A GitHub variant of symptoms-and-root-causes would need `sub_issues: parent` on a dedicated board (see Findings).

findings: **Coexistence is not safe on one board, and the design's `sub_issues` setting does not by itself make it safe across two.** The design says a `sub_issues: parent` source is opt-in and default membership is unchanged. Measured: a default source reads a `parent` source's top ticket as a project and flattens its hierarchy; an edge added or removed from either side changes the other's view; and because `Auto-add sub-issues to project` is enabled by default, adding a parent ticket to a default-meaning board pulls its descendants onto that board within 30 s. An issue has exactly one parent across both meanings. The design should require a `parent` source's board to be separate, name that an issue on a default board will read as a project, and consider refusing a write that would put a `parent` ticket on a default board.

**GitHub limits are 8 levels (a root plus 7 layers) and 100 children per parent**, as GitHub documents them and as refused before the probe was stopped. The design's 'destination limits fail only their edge' covers this; the `parent` kind's limits should be stated.

**A 60-alias GitHub mutation answered 504 and still landed 58 of 60 writes.** Aliased batches of at most 30 per document are the measured safe size for `addRelatesTo`, and a retry after an error must be idempotent, which `addRelatesTo` proved to be (435) and Linear's `issueRelationCreate` proved to be in either direction (121–122).

**The secondary limiter, not the point budget, binds sustained relation writes.** 123 `createIssue` and 119 `addSubIssue` aliases in 42 documents over four minutes tripped a 403. A cycle that creates tickets and writes parents and links must pace at the plan level, not only per document.

**Metadata-plus-section does not survive a whole-body rewrite on either tracker.** That end's links vanish while the other end's stand, so the two ends disagree. The design's metadata-on-both-ends authority needs a stated repair: a read that sees one end's edge without the other's should either restore it or report it, and a `partial` outcome alone does not describe this case.

**The `## Links` parser must accept what Linear normalizes**: `- ` bullets are stored as `* ` and blank lines change. Heading, bold, link, code span and HTML-comment slot are preserved, as far as an API edit shows; a human edit in Linear's editor is unverified.

**`duplicate` is status-bearing on both trackers.** GitHub marks one only by closing the issue, and Linear moves it to the `Duplicate` state. The design admits only `relates-to` and `related` as native words; if a team wants a native duplicate mirror it needs a word and a stated status effect, otherwise duplicate stays metadata only (the recommendation in the matrix).

**Native relates-to and related are symmetric.** The design's directed `caused-by` is therefore carried only in metadata, as designed; the native mirror cannot express direction, and on Linear a create in the opposite direction returns the same relation, so a mirror cannot record which end asserted it.

**`deleteIssue` can answer success and leave the issue.** An issue that held 100 sub-issues (`#6094`) stayed OPEN and read back after three accepted deletes (663, 705, 721), its sub-issues already gone. A cleanup of a parent ticket must verify the delete rather than trust the success, and a design that deletes a parent may need to delete its children first or accept a closed-and-stamped remainder.

**The arithmetic in the budget evidence is met but rests on 1 point per mutation document.** Mutations do not report `rateLimit.cost`; the 1 is the quiet-window `x-ratelimit-used` delta (requests 18, 19, 23, 53), and larger deltas in the log are other consumers of a shared token. The loopback-measured budget therefore should use the documented per-document cost.
